source.title: Up from Slavery
source.attribution: Booker T. Washington, Up from Slavery, Standard Ebooks, public domain

cards.title: Do the humble task so well that no one can fault it
cards.body:
When Booker T. Washington reached Hampton Institute after a long journey, tired, penniless and travel-worn, the head teacher hesitated to admit him. Then she asked him to sweep a classroom. He swept it three times and dusted every surface four times, sensing his future depended on it. She couldn't find a speck of dirt, and he was admitted.

He later urged people to do a common thing in an uncommon way, so thoroughly that nobody could improve on it. A small job done with unusual care is often the clearest evidence of what someone will do with a bigger one.
cards.quote: In a degree I felt that my whole future life depended upon the thoroughness with which I cleaned that room, and I was determined to do it so well that no one could find any fault with the job.
cards.apply_it: Pick one routine task today and do it noticeably better than required, as if someone were judging your future on it.

quiz.question: How did Washington win his place at Hampton Institute?
options: By sweeping and dusting a classroom with great thoroughness
By paying his fees in advance
quiz.explanation: He later called the sweeping of that room his 'college examination', and the teacher could not find a speck of dirt.

cards.title: Measure success by the obstacles you've overcome
cards.body:
Washington, born into slavery, wrote that success should be judged less by the position someone reaches than by the obstacles they overcame on the way. Two people at the same level may have travelled very different distances to get there.

He also saw that hard struggle builds a strength and confidence that a smooth path doesn't. This is a healthier yardstick than comparing yourself with people who started with more. It doesn't excuse the barriers anyone faces, but it gives you credit for the ground you've actually covered.
cards.quote: I have learned that success is to be measured not so much by the position that one has reached in life as by the obstacles which he has overcome while trying to succeed.
cards.apply_it: Write down three obstacles you've overcome to get where you are. Reread them the next time you compare yourself with someone else.

quiz.question: How did Washington think success should be measured?
options: By the obstacles overcome while trying to succeed
quiz.explanation: He judged success less by the position reached than by the obstacles overcome along the way.

cards.title: When the third attempt fails, find a way to fund the fourth
cards.body:
At Tuskegee, Washington wanted students to make their own bricks for the school's new buildings. Brickmaking turned out to be far harder than he expected. The first kiln failed, then the second, then a third. Teachers urged him to give up, the students were discouraged, and he had no money left.

He pawned his watch for fifteen dollars, rallied the team and tried again. The fourth kiln worked. He never got the watch back and never regretted it. Projects often fail at the point where people stop trying, not where the idea stops being good.
cards.quote: I returned to Tuskegee, and, with the help of the fifteen dollars, rallied our rather demoralized and discouraged forces and began a fourth attempt to make bricks. This time, I am glad to say, we were successful.
cards.locator: X. A Harder Task Than Making Bricks… ¶10
cards.apply_it: Think of a project you've shelved after a couple of failures. What could you put on the line for one more, better-planned attempt?

quiz.question: What did Washington do after three brick kilns failed?
options: Pawned his watch to fund a fourth attempt
quiz.explanation: With no money left, he pawned his watch for fifteen dollars, and the fourth kiln succeeded.

cards.title: Lead by picking up the axe yourself
cards.body:
In the early days at Tuskegee, Washington wanted students to clear land for crops. Many, some of them former schoolteachers, felt manual labour was beneath an educated person and held back. Instead of lecturing them, he took an axe every afternoon after classes and led the way into the woods himself.

Once they saw he wasn't ashamed to work, they joined in with more enthusiasm, and together they cleared about twenty acres. People follow what leaders do far more than what they say. A manager who handles the unglamorous jobs sets the standard better than any memo.
cards.quote: When they saw that I was not afraid or ashamed to work, they began to assist with more enthusiasm.
cards.locator: VIII. Teaching School in a Stable and a… ¶29
cards.apply_it: Identify an unglamorous task your team or household avoids. Do it yourself this week, without comment.

quiz.question: How did Washington get reluctant students to clear land?
options: He led the work himself with an axe every afternoon
quiz.explanation: Seeing him work without shame changed their minds more than any argument could.

cards.title: Speak only when you have something worth saying
cards.body:
Washington became one of the most sought-after speakers of his day, yet he believed you wrong both yourself and your audience when you speak just for the sake of it. Only when you're convinced you have something that will help someone should you stand up, and then conviction matters more than polished technique.

His mentor, General Armstrong, gave him another rule: give them an idea for every word. In meetings, presentations and posts, the same test applies. Before speaking, ask what you want the listener to take away. If there's no clear answer, stay quiet or keep it short.
cards.quote: I do not believe that one should speak unless, deep down in his heart, he feels convinced that he has a message to deliver.
cards.locator: XV. The Secret of Success in Public Speaking ¶16
cards.apply_it: Before your next meeting or presentation, write in one sentence what you want people to take away. Cut anything that doesn't serve it.

quiz.question: What advice did General Armstrong give Washington about speaking?
options: Always speak for at least an hour
Give them an idea for every word
quiz.explanation: 'Give them an idea for every word' was the one piece of advice Washington remembered and tried to follow ever after.

cards.title: Treat a small first 'yes' as a chance to prove yourself
cards.body:
The first time the railroad magnate Collis Huntington gave to Tuskegee, it was two dollars. Washington didn't resent the small amount. He resolved to show, through concrete results, that the school deserved more. Over about a dozen years Huntington's gifts grew as the school's usefulness grew, until he gave fifty thousand dollars.

Washington insisted this was hard work, not luck. Whether it's a first client, a small order or a trial project, a modest start is an invitation. Deliver visibly, keep the relationship warm, and bigger trust tends to follow.
cards.quote: When Mr. Huntington gave me the first two dollars, I did not blame him for not giving me more, but made up my mind that I was going to convince him by tangible results that we were worthy of larger gifts.
cards.apply_it: Think of a small opportunity you've been given recently. What one tangible result could you deliver to earn a bigger one?

quiz.question: How did Washington respond to Huntington's first gift of two dollars?
options: He asked for more straight away
He set out to prove with results that the school deserved more
quiz.explanation: He didn't blame Huntington for giving little; he worked for years to show tangible results, and the gifts grew to fifty thousand dollars.
